translation: In the winter of 1993, the most important thing for me was that my father returned, a week before my mother's wedding.
One afternoon in December, he came to find me at school.
I rushed all the way to the gate only to see him standing outside smoking a cigarette and looking through the iron railings from afar.
He wore a black trench coat with an upright collar covering half of his face.
For some unknown reason, I sensed he was not doing well even without getting a clear look at him and that brought tears to my eyes.
I never thought that my mother would consider remarrying.
Perhaps subconsciously, I believed she should continue to feel pain due to my father's departure, just like me.
Moreover, I felt she lacked the ability to find happiness again.
While this may have been true, happiness had the ability to find her.
After all, as a beautiful woman, she did not have to make much effort; all she needed was simply stand still and let things happen around her.
I still remember, that year's winter was exceptionally long.
Halfway through April, and the jasmine had not yet bloomed.
Our parents' divorce had you in such a low state.
We didn't have any new games for a long time, and at dusk we would sit aimlessly on the roof of the tower of the dead.
Amongst the body parts strewn around our yard, there were several more arms than before.
Using hooks and sticks we gathered them together to form something that resembled Thousand-Handed Guanyin (a statue form of Buddha).
Actually, my father knew nothing about doing business.
He was just trying to work with a distant cousin whom he didn't know well.
My grandmother had a sister who had moved to Beijing years ago and later married and gave birth there.
This cousin was her eldest son, who has always been considered an outlier in our entire family.
You mentioned before that everyone has a time when their fate seems to suddenly be reined in.
I think mine was when I was eight years old.
In autumn of that year, my father left Jinan and went to Beijing alone.
Since then, I haven't had a home anymore.
I had no intention of keeping the appointment.
Whatever the reason, I thought there was no longer any need for us to see each other again.
Sitting on the sofa chain-smoking, as it got darker and darker, there was suddenly a knock at the door.
The water delivery boy stood at the entrance with his water bucket, saying he was delivering water to a household in the western suburbs.
He wore a dirtied grey woolen hat and looked absent-minded.
Our conversation was very difficult.
Each silence made me feel a tightness in my chest and I could only think of ending our meeting as quickly as possible.
You seemed to sense this but continued to try and find topics of conversation.
As the tea cooled down, the vapor in the room dissipated, you finally stood up to leave.
No sooner than I had shut the door and exhaled a sigh of relief, did the doorbell ring again.
It was you, standing at my doorstep asking me to visit Xiao Bai Lou later tonight.
Before I even had the chance to decline your invitation, you had already disappeared out of sight down the stairs.
I walked into the kitchen and turned off the stove.
Half of the water had already evaporated, filling the entire room with a foggy haze.
You sat down uncomfortably and watched as I poured tea.
"Do you still live with your grandma and aunt?" you asked.
I told you that grandma has passed away and now it's just me living with my aunt.
"She never got married?", you questioned further, to which I responded simply,"Yes.

The white breath coming out of your mouth, your curly hair ruffled by the wind, and the slight tremble in your knees beneath the hem of your coat all convince me that you're really here before me now, not merely a continuation from a previous dream.
It has been eighteen years; it's no surprise if I can't recognize you.
You haven't put on makeup—your pale face is slightly puffy but at least you haven't disappointed everyone by growing up to be beautiful.
Although, that heart-shaped face is cloaked in gloominess—revealing an expression typical of someone who's lived in a big city for too long.
You asked me if you looked different than what I imagined.
I just smiled ambiguously because truthfully, I had never imagined how you would look all grown up.
For me, everything related to you has already been filed away and sealed with wax—which might sound hurtful—but honestly speaking, I didn't have any expectations to see you again.
I opened my eyes.
You were standing in the doorway.
I didn't know how long you had been there-probably long enough to have seen even how I laugh in my dreams, the sorrow upon waking, and my appearance at its weakest moment.
Cheng Gong, you whispered my name, your voice gruff as though you hadn't spoken for a very long time.
It was about to snow; the weather was getting worst and it was pitch black inside our house.
The water on the stove boiled with gulping sounds resonating throughout the room.
I looked closely at you for a while decidedly sure that I didn't recognize you but under this dim light, something told me this stranger standing before me had deep ties with my life.
It's a creepy sensation that sent chills running down my spine.
Racking through different cards of memories swiftly in my mind but found nothing related to your face until finally; then you said: "You are Li Jiaqi".
